messages.text:
I have found a simple way to reduce temperatures of both the ASIC and VRM on the lHammer BC04. I wanted to tell you so you can pass it on to other customers. I have a cheap USB fan which has 3 speeds. If I position it behind the BC04 pointing slightly up on the lowest setting it reduces both temperatures by several degrees Celsius.

Andrew T.

Hi Andrew,

Thank you for this, and for taking the trouble to write it up. That is a genuinely good tip and it matches what we see on these boards.

The reason it works so well is where you have put it. The B.04 pulls its air in at the back, and left to itself it tends to re-breathe its own warm exhaust, especially sitting on a desk or a shelf where the hot air rolls back around. A slow stream of room air aimed slightly upward into that intake does two things at once: it gives the fan cooler air to work with, and it breaks up the pocket of warm air hanging around the board. The V. stage benefits more than the ASIC does, which is exactly the pattern you saw, because that stage sits in the slower-moving air behind the heatsink rather than in the main duct. And keeping the USB fan on its lowest setting is the right instinct, since too much cross-flow can actually disturb the main fan's path rather than help it.

Worth adding for anyone else who tries it: it is extra intake air, not extra static pressure, so it will not rescue a unit with a clogged heatsink or a failing fan, and it is no substitute for a bit of clear space around the unit. If your VRM has come down a few degrees from where it was sitting just under 75C, you have headroom to put some of that clock back and chase the 5.5TH you were after, watching the VRM as you go.

I have passed your tip to JD so it can go into what we tell other BC04 owners. If you fancy sharing it with the wider crowd, the Harlo Discord at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf is where this sort of thing spreads fastest, and JD is @nullhashrate there.

Thanks again Andrew, genuinely useful.

Hal, HeliumDeploy Technical Support

The vrm is between 68.0 and 68.5c and the ASIC is at 60c and I am getting 5.4TH/s. I may try and get 5.5 in a few days. The other benefit is it runs very quiet.

Andrew T.

Hi Andrew,

Those are lovely numbers. A VRM at 68C and the ASIC at 60C is a comfortable place to live, and dropping the VRM around seven degrees from where it was sitting is a bigger win than the fan tip has any right to deliver.

The quiet is the other half of the same trick. Cooler intake air means the main fan's auto curve has less work to do, so it settles lower, and fan noise climbs steeply with RPM. A slow USB fan moving the same air at a fraction of the speed is simply a quieter way to shift it.

On the 5.5TH, you have the headroom now, so go at it gently when you get round to it. Raise the frequency one step at a time rather than touching voltage first, leave it an hour at each step so the VRM has time to reach its real steady temperature, and watch the pool side rather than the local figure. If the local hashrate climbs but the pool number does not follow over a few hours, or you start seeing hardware errors or rejects creep in, that step was too far and the one below it was your limit. I would treat the mid seventies as the line you do not want the VRM to cross for a long run, so you have maybe five or six degrees of budget to spend.

One small thing worth knowing: ambient temperature will move all of this. As the weather turns colder your room air does some of the work for you, and come summer the same settings will read several degrees warmer. So if you tune to the edge now, expect to give a little back later in the year.

Enjoy it, and thanks again for the tip.

Hal, HeliumDeploy Technical Support
